rows.subtype: Approach: safety plan with a helpline number for a crisis [Action]
rows.description: With a counsellor, the person writes a short list of warning signs, calming steps, people to call and a national helpline number to use if things feel unsafe. Preparing in advance means the steps are ready when thinking is clouded.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning, forward planning
related mind states: detachment, calm, trust

rows.subtype: Approach: behavioural activation with small planned pleasures [Action]
rows.description: Working with a counsellor, the student schedules one pleasant activity daily, such as a short walk or a call with a friend, even when motivation is low. Action can come before the mood lifts.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: wait for it to pass through sleeping and scrolling [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person sleeps late, scrolls on the phone and stays in bed, hoping the mood lifts alone. The routine keeps energy low, and weeks pass before anyone notices.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: identify the rule and value at stake [Thinking]
rows.description: Asked by a manager to backdate a document for a client audit, the junior analyst asks what it would mean if the record were false, and recalls company policy and personal integrity. Naming the principle clears the fog of pressure.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, impulsive action, mental simulation

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of the refusal conversation [Thinking]
rows.description: The employee imagines the manager's reactions and prepares calm wording such as offering to fix the delay honestly instead of falsifying records. Rehearsal makes it easier to stay steady under pressure.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, impulsive action, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: comply quietly to avoid conflict [Pitfall]
rows.description: Afraid of losing the job, the employee backdates the document and tells no one. The fear of consequences is real, but the person now carries the risk of an audit and the guilt, and may be asked again.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: impulsive action, mental simulation, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: offer a lawful alternative that meets the goal [Action]
rows.description: The employee tells the manager the paper cannot be backdated but suggests a note explaining the delay and offers to prepare it that afternoon. Solving the underlying need can defuse the conflict without breaking rules.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, impulsive action, mental simulation, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: document the request and check the code of conduct [Action]
rows.description: The employee writes down the date and words of the request, reads the ethics policy and asks a trusted senior how such matters are handled. A record and a reference protect both honesty and job.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, impulsive action, mental simulation, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: escalate to HR or the ethics channel if pressure continues [Revision]
rows.description: When the manager repeats the request, the employee moves from private refusal to a written report to HR or the ethics helpline, keeping details factual. Escalation is used when direct handling does not work.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, impulsive action, mental simulation, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: assume the boss must be right due to seniority [Pitfall]
rows.description: A new joiner reasons that a senior person would not ask for something wrong and follows the instruction without checking. Deference replaces judgement, and responsibility is not removed for the person who signs.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, mental simulation, values-first planning
